text:
The ink wasn’t just faded; it was *alive*, pulsing with a faint, bioluminescent violet. I didn’t need glasses to read the cursive script; the words crawled directly into my peripheral vision, whispering instructions in a dialect of forgotten grief.

*“Take three tears of regret,”* the card demanded. *“Harvest them at dawn from the eyes of those who have lost everything but hope.”*

I laughed, thinking it a prank by my great-aunt’s eccentric estate lawyer. But when I opened the pantry, the air smelled of ozone and old roses. The flour bag was filled not with wheat, but with ground-up memories—fine, white dust that tickled my nose with images of first kisses and final goodbyes.

Following the recipe, I mixed the memory-flour with the tear-harvested liquid. The dough rose instantly, breathing like a sleeping animal. When I baked it, the oven didn’t heat up; it cooled down, freezing time inside the glass window. The resulting loaf wasn’t bread. It was a door.

As I sliced into the crust, steam escaped, forming shapes of people long dead. They stepped out, solidifying in the kitchen light, hungry not for food, but for closure. My great-aunt stood among them, smiling softly. She hadn’t died forty years ago. She had simply been waiting for someone to cook her back into existence.
